summary: This informational document specifies a mechanism and document format that lets WebDAV servers send mounting information to a WebDAV client. Clicking a link can then open an editable view of the server. It relies only on the MIME type dispatch available in browsers.

eli5.summary: Clicking a link to a shared folder usually just shows a page. This describes a special file so the click opens the folder like one on your own computer.

subtitle: A way to open WebDAV servers directly from browser links using a special file format

tldr.problem: When users click a link in a web browser that points to a WebDAV server, they usually see an HTML page instead of getting an editable view with drag-and-drop support that a native WebDAV client could provide.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies a platform-neutral XML format and MIME type (application/davmount+xml) that WebDAV servers can send. When a browser receives this file, it dispatches it to the user's WebDAV client, which then opens the server directory for editing.
tldr.outcome: Users can now click a link in their browser and have their WebDAV client open immediately with an editable, drag-and-drop interface, improving the experience of accessing shared document collections.

today: RFC 4709 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted. The application/davmount+xml media type and mount document format remain the standard way to launch WebDAV clients from web browser links.

sections.title: The Problem with WebDAV in Browsers
sections.content:
WebDAV (Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning) is a protocol built on top of HTTP that lets users edit documents on a web server, not just read them. A WebDAV server can be operated from a browser's HTML interface, but this provides only basic viewing and uploading.

Users often want to switch from the browser view to a native WebDAV client, which offers full authoring features: drag-and-drop file manipulation, properties dialogs, version control, and other capabilities that HTTP browsers alone cannot provide. This RFC solves this problem using a mechanism based on MIME type dispatch—the same system that makes web browsers know to open PDF files with a PDF reader.

A common use case is educational institutions that run WebDAV servers as document-sharing hubs. Students should be able to click a link in the university portal and have their locker appear as an editable folder on their desktop.
sections.eli5: A WebDAV server holds files you can edit online, but web browsers can only show a basic page. This lets you click a link and open the real folder view instead, with all the editing tools.

sections.title: The WebDAV Mount Document Format
sections.content:
A WebDAV mount request uses XML format with a standard MIME type registered as application/davmount+xml. The elements use the namespace http://purl.org/NET/webdav/mount.

The dm:mount element acts as a container for the following child elements:

  • dm:url: The mandatory HTTP URL of the WebDAV collection to mount. This is the base address of the shared folder.
  • dm:open: Optional. Specifies a child collection within the base URL to display immediately. Its value is concatenated with the base URL.
  • dm:username: Optional. The name of the currently authenticated principal. Allows the client to match mount points for different users or to provide a default for authentication.

Element ordering is irrelevant, and extension elements may be added as needed.
sections.eli5: The file is XML with a few parts: the base folder address (required), the subfolder to open right away (optional), and the username logging in (optional). Programs read this simple format and know what to do.

sections.title: How the Mounting Workflow Operates
sections.content:
The workflow has four steps. First, a user retrieves an HTML page from the WebDAV server using a standard browser. Second, the server's HTML contains a hyperlink pointing to a special "davmount" document. Third, when the user clicks this link, the browser downloads the davmount file. Fourth, the browser's MIME type handler recognizes the application/davmount+xml type and dispatches the file to the system's registered WebDAV client application.

The WebDAV client then parses the XML, reads the URL and optional open path, and connects to the server. If an open element was provided, the client displays that specific collection. If only a URL was given, the client displays the root of the mount point.

This mechanism is completely platform-neutral and works with any combination of browser and WebDAV client software, requiring only that the operating system has a MIME type handler registered for davmount files.
sections.eli5: You visit a website and click a link. The link downloads a tiny XML file. Your computer recognizes the file type and hands it to your WebDAV program, which opens the folder view right away.

sections.title: Security Concerns with WebDAV Mounting
sections.content:
The security considerations of HTTP, WebDAV, and XML all apply to this specification. Implementers must be particularly careful with the dm:open element. It MUST NOT be used to initiate actions beyond displaying the contents of a WebDAV collection. Supporting document opening could be abused to trick users into letting the operating system execute arbitrary code.

The optional dm:username element can expose user names. In some contexts, user name information is security-sensitive. Servers SHOULD either omit usernames or use access controls to restrict access to mount documents that include them. If a username is present, servers should set appropriate HTTP headers (like Cache-Control: private) to prevent public caching of the mount document.

All other security considerations from RFC 2518 (WebDAV) and RFC 3470 (XML in IETF protocols) also apply.
sections.eli5: The open command should only show folders, never run programs or scripts. And usernames in the file should be kept private, not cached by public caches.

sections.title: MIME Type Registration
sections.content:
The specification registers a new MIME type with IANA:

  • Type name: application
  • Subtype name: davmount+xml
  • File extension: .davmount
  • Charset parameter: Optional; has the same semantics as the charset parameter of application/xml (RFC 3023)
  • Encoding considerations: Identical to application/xml
  • Intended usage: COMMON

There are no known interoperability issues. The applications that use this media type include SAP Netweaver Knowledge Management and Xythos Drive WebDAV client.
sections.eli5: The official label application/davmount+xml is registered with IANA. Files use the .davmount extension. This makes it official that this media type exists and how to handle it.
